screens.title: Embracing Abstract Classes and Interfaces
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we explore two complementary tools for designing object-oriented systems in Java: abstract classes and interfaces. You will learn why we declare some types abstract, how abstract methods enforce subclass behavior, and how interfaces define reusable behavioral contracts. We'll examine practical examples, like a Shape hierarchy that defers area calculations to concrete shapes, and an Edible/Washable pair of interfaces that let unrelated classes share behavior. You'll also see how interfaces evolved in Java 8 to include default and static methods, and why that matters for A P I design. By the end of this chapter, you will understand when to provide a shared base implementation in an abstract class and when to expose a capability through an interface so classes can adopt it freely. We'll ground ideas with a hands-on payment processing exercise that demonstrates polymorphism: an Order uses a PaymentGateway contract to process payments without knowing gateway details. Notice how these patterns increase modularity, reduce duplication, and make code easier to extend. As you learn, ask yourself: would this behavior be better as a core identity of the type, or as an optional capability that many types may share?

Embracing Abstract Classes and Interfaces
Designing clear contracts and flexible hierarchies in Java to improve extensibility and reuse.

This chapter shows how abstract classes provide shared state and partial implementations, while interfaces define behavior contracts. You'll practice both styles and learn Java 8+ interface features that make interfaces more expressive.

Why this matters: clean contracts reduce coupling and make code easier to extend without breaking existing implementations.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this set of objectives we make your outcomes explicit. First, you will learn to define and implement abstract classes: that means declaring a class as abstract, providing fields and concrete methods where appropriate, and declaring abstract methods that subclasses must implement. Practically, you'll apply this to examples like a Shape base class whose subclasses compute area. Second, you will create and use interfaces to describe behavior contracts. This includes writing interfaces, having classes implement them, and using those types polymorphically. Third, you will learn to differentiate when a design needs an abstract class versus an interface by examining their capabilities, inheritance rules, and common use cases. Finally, you'll begin to use Java 8+ interface features, implementing default and static methods when an interface benefits from a shared helper. Each skill reduces coupling and increases extensibility. As you progress, watch for the difference between owning state and declaring behavior: that distinction guides whether you choose an abstract class or an interface.

screens.title: What is an Abstract Class?
screens.narratorSegment: An abstract class is a blueprint that cannot be instantiated directly and exists to be extended by concrete subclasses. It can contain fields, constructors, concrete methods with implementations, and abstract methods without bodies. Abstract methods declare a contract that subclasses must fulfill; if a subclass does not provide implementations for all inherited abstract methods, it must itself be declared abstract. This pattern is useful when there is a strong 'is-a' relationship and shared state or default behaviors belong on the base type. For example, a Shape abstract class can hold a color field, a constructor to set color, and a concrete displayColor method, while leaving calculateArea undefined so each concrete shape supplies its own formula. A common misconception is thinking abstract classes are only for uninstantiable objects — instead, emphasize they capture shared state and partial logic so subclasses avoid duplication. In practice, use abstract classes to centralize fields and default methods that truly belong to the base identity. Consider whether subclasses will share implementation or only behavior; that decision guides whether to make a base class abstract. What is an Abstract Class? means abstract classes bundle shared state and partial behavior while forcing subclasses to implement missing specifics.. In practical terms, a partially implemented type that defines a shared base and enforces contracts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › What is an Abstract Class?
Definition

An abstract class cannot be instantiated. It may include fields, constructors, concrete methods, and abstract methods that subclasses must implement. Use it when a set of types shares identity and some implementation.

Features
  • Can have constructors and instance variables.
  • May declare abstract methods that lack bodies.
  • Encourages shared implementation among subclasses.
Common misconception
Abstract classes are not merely uninstantiable; they are design tools to hold common state and behavior for related concrete types.
Concrete example
Shape is an abstract class with a color field, a constructor, a concrete displayColor method, and an abstract calculateArea method. Circle and Rectangle extend Shape and implement calculateArea differently.
Key Takeaway

Use abstract classes when types share state or default behavior and you want to force specific methods to be implemented by subclasses.

screens.title: Shape Example: Abstract Methods and Concrete Methods
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a concrete Shape example to see how abstract and concrete members coexist. The Shape class declares a protected color field and a constructor to initialize it. It declares an abstract method calculateArea, which has no body and signals that each concrete subclass must provide its own formula. At the same time Shape provides concrete methods like displayColor and getColor so subclasses inherit common behavior. A key point is that declaring even a single abstract method forces the class to be marked abstract. This design keeps area calculation specific to each shape while sharing color handling across all shapes. One misconception is thinking abstract methods are optional; they are not — concrete subclasses must implement them or be abstract themselves. In practice, this pattern reduces duplication because Circle and Rectangle inherit displayColor instead of reimplementing it. Consider how a new Triangle subclass would only add its own area logic while reusing Shape's color and display methods. This balance of enforced contracts and reusable logic is the main strength of abstract classes. Shape Example: Abstract Methods and Concrete Methods means abstract methods enforce shape-specific behavior; concrete methods share common functionality.. In practical terms, inspecting a shape base class that mixes abstract and concrete behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Shape Example
Shape.java (abstract)
public abstract class Shape {
  protected String color;

  public Shape(String color) {
    this.color = color;
  }

  // abstract method: no body
  public abstract double calculateArea();

  // concrete method
  public void displayColor() {
    System.out.println("This shape is " + color);
  }

  public String getColor() {
    return color;
  }
}
Teaching notes
  • Protected fields allow subclasses to access shared state directly.
  • An abstract method like calculateArea enforces that subclasses supply the implementation.
  • Concrete helper methods reduce duplicated code across subclasses.
Misconception
Marking a class abstract is not a weakness — it's a deliberate design to separate shared behavior from specifics.
Key Takeaway

Use abstract classes when you need shared state and you want to force concrete subclasses to implement specific methods.

screens.title: Concrete Subclasses: Circle and Rectangle
screens.narratorSegment: Now let's examine concrete subclasses that extend an abstract class. Circle and Rectangle inherit Shape's color field and constructor behavior while providing their own state and concrete implementations of calculateArea. Circle keeps a radius field and overrides calculateArea to return pi times radius squared. Rectangle stores length and width and overrides calculateArea to return length times width. These subclasses demonstrate how the abstract base enforces a contract while allowing each subclass to manage its own details. A common misunderstanding is thinking subclasses must replicate base constructors; in fact they call super to reuse base initialization. Another pitfall is forgetting to annotate overrides; while optional, the override annotation helps catch signature mismatches at compile time. The benefit here is clear: code that expects a Shape can call calculateArea without knowing whether it’s a Circle or a Rectangle, enabling polymorphic code and easier extension when new shapes are added. Concrete Subclasses: Circle and Rectangle means concrete subclasses must implement abstract methods and can extend the base with their own fields and behavior.. In practical terms, how subclasses implement abstract methods and add their own state. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Circle & Rectangle
Circle.java
public class Circle extends Shape {
  private double radius;
  private static final double PI = Math.PI;

  public Circle(String color, double radius) {
    super(color);
    this.radius = radius;
  }

  @Override
  public double calculateArea() {
    return PI * radius * radius;
  }

  public double getRadius() {
    return radius;
  }
}
Rectangle.java
public class Rectangle extends Shape {
  private double length;
  private double width;

  public Rectangle(String color, double length, double width) {
    super(color);
    this.length = length;
    this.width = width;
  }

  @Override
  public double calculateArea() {
    return length * width;
  }

  public double getLength() { return length; }
  public double getWidth() { return width; }
}
Practical note
Call super in constructors to initialize base fields and use @Override to avoid signature mistakes.

screens.title: Interfaces: Contracts for Behavior
screens.narratorSegment: An interface is a contract that specifies behavior a class promises to provide. Historically, interfaces only declared abstract methods and constants. Since Java 8, interfaces can also contain default methods with implementations and static helper methods. Classes implement interfaces and must provide concrete implementations for all abstract methods the interface declares. A major advantage of interfaces is that a class can implement multiple interfaces, gaining multiple types without the limitations of single class inheritance. Think of interfaces as 'can-do' capabilities: for example, an Edible interface asks for a howToEat method, while Washable declares a wash method and includes a default dry implementation. One misconception is treating interfaces as an alternative place to store state: interfaces may only declare constants; they don’t hold instance fields. Use interfaces when unrelated classes should share a behavior contract, like both Apple and Chicken being Edible, without forcing them into the same class hierarchy. Interfaces: Contracts for Behavior means interfaces declare behavior contracts and let classes adopt capabilities without committing to a shared class lineage.. In practical terms, defining capabilities without imposing implementation details. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Interfaces
What an interface is

An interface defines method signatures and constants that classes promise to implement. Use interfaces for capabilities that can apply across unrelated classes and to enable multiple inheritance of type.

Capability example
Edible declares howToEat; Washable declares wash, and supplies a default dry method. Classes choose which contracts to implement.
Why interfaces matter
  • Allow multiple types for a class, enabling flexible APIs.
  • Keep implementations decoupled from usage via interface types.
  • Support API evolution with default and static methods.
Common Pitfall

Don’t use interfaces to store instance state. If you need shared fields and default logic tied to identity, prefer an abstract class.

screens.title: Edible and Washable Interfaces with Implementations
screens.narratorSegment: Let's inspect a pair of interfaces and how a class implements them. Edible defines a howToEat method to describe how to consume a food item. Washable declares wash and provides a default dry implementation plus a static helper for instructions. An Apple class implements both Edible and Washable, providing howToEat and wash while using the default dry method. Chicken implements Edible only, so it cannot be washed without implementing Washable. This example demonstrates multiple inheritance of type: a single class can be both Edible and Washable, letting code depend on those capabilities rather than concrete classes. A common misconception is assuming default means optional in all cases; default provides a ready implementation but implementing classes can override it if they need a different behavior. Also note static methods on interfaces belong to the interface itself and are called on the interface, not an instance. These features give interface designers more flexibility to evolve APIs while staying backward compatible. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Edible & Washable
Edible & Washable (interface snippets)
public interface Edible {
  String howToEat(); // implicitly public abstract
}

public interface Washable {
  void wash();

  default void dry() {
    System.out.println("Drying the item after washing.");
  }

  static void printWashingInstructions() {
    System.out.println("Always wash with mild soap and rinse thoroughly.");
  }
}
Apple and Chicken
class Apple implements Edible, Washable {
  @Override
  public String howToEat() { return "Bite into the crisp apple."; }

  @Override
  public void wash() { System.out.println("Washing the apple under running water."); }
}

class Chicken implements Edible {
  @Override
  public String howToEat() { return "Cook thoroughly and then eat."; }
}
Note
Default methods let interfaces provide safe defaults so existing implementers don't break when new behavior is added.

screens.title: Abstract Class vs Interface — Side-by-Side
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the difference between abstract classes and interfaces is essential for making good design choices. Abstract classes allow instance fields, constructors, and a mix of abstract and concrete methods; they support a single inheritance chain via extends. Interfaces cannot have instance fields; their fields are implicitly public static final, and classes implement them to agree to certain behaviors. Since Java 8, interfaces may include default and static methods, but they still lack instance state. Use an abstract class when several related types share common state and partial implementation — like Vehicle as a base for Car and Motorcycle. Use an interface when you want to express a capability that many unrelated types can implement — like Runnable or Washable. A common source of confusion is thinking interfaces are always the more flexible choice; if you need shared fields or constructor logic, an abstract class fits better. Also remember a class can implement multiple interfaces, enabling multiple inheritance of type, while it can only extend a single class. Reflect on whether you need shared identity or shared capability to choose the correct construct.

keyIdea.title: Choosing guidance
keyIdea.text: Pick abstract classes for shared identity and implementation; pick interfaces for cross-cutting capabilities and multiple type inheritance.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Abstract Class vs Interface
Abstract Class
  • Can have constructors and instance variables.
  • Can mix abstract and concrete methods.
  • Supports single inheritance (extend one class).
  • Best for strong 'is-a' hierarchies with shared state.
Interface
  • Cannot have instance fields; fields are public static final.
  • May declare abstract, default, and static methods.
  • Classes can implement multiple interfaces (multiple inheritance of type).
  • Best for 'can-do' capabilities across unrelated classes.
Designer checklist
  1. If you need shared fields or constructor logic, prefer an abstract class.
  2. If you need multiple types or cross-cutting behavior, prefer interfaces.
  3. Use default methods sparingly to evolve interfaces without breaking implementers.

screens.title: Rules and Common Mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: There are a few recurring errors beginners make when using abstract classes and interfaces. First, trying to instantiate an abstract class produces a compile-time error because abstract classes are incomplete blueprints. Always instantiate a concrete subclass instead. Second, failing to implement all inherited abstract methods will force the subclass to be abstract or cause a compilation error. When you extend an abstract class or implement an interface, double-check that every abstract method is implemented or mark the subclass abstract. Third, confusing extends with implements can lead to incorrect declarations: extends is for class inheritance, while implements is for interface contracts. Fourth, misunderstanding default methods can cause surprise: default provides a fallback implementation but can be overridden; it still belongs to the interface's public A P I. Follow a simple process to avoid these mistakes: identify which behaviors need state, choose abstract class or interface accordingly, implement all required methods, and use @Override annotations to catch signature mismatches. These small checks prevent common compilation failures and keep your design intentional. screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity demonstrates polymorphism using an interface PaymentGateway and concrete gateway classes. The PaymentGateway interface declares a processPayment method that returns a boolean indicating success. Concrete gateways like CreditCardPaymentGateway and PayPalPaymentGateway implement this method with their own processing logic. screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the core concepts to remember. An abstract class is a base that cannot be instantiated, can have fields and constructors, and mixes abstract methods with concrete implementations to share behavior. An abstract method declares a required behavior without an implementation and forces subclasses to implement it. An interface is a behavioral contract that classes implement; it now supports default and static methods which help evolve APIs safely. Remember that interface fields are public static final constants; interfaces do not hold instance state. Multiple inheritance of type is possible because a class may implement multiple interfaces, allowing it to be treated as several types. Keep these distinctions in mind when you design: choose abstract classes when shared state and identity matter; choose interfaces when you need composable capabilities across unrelated types. These choices help keep systems modular and easier to extend.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.narratorSegment: Keep three essentials close as you write Java code. First, abstract methods require implementation: any abstract method declared in a base type must be implemented by concrete subclasses or the subclass must be abstract. Second, use interfaces to express capabilities and enable a class to play multiple roles, such as Edible and Washable; this reduces coupling between producers and consumers of behavior. Third, Java 8's default and static methods let interfaces evolve safely, offering shared behavior or helpers without forcing all implementers to change. When you design, ask whether shared data is needed or if you only need to promise a behavior. That simple question guides whether a class should be abstract or whether an interface is the better tool. These three reminders will help you design clearer, more extensible object-oriented systems.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we explore two complementary tools for designing object-oriented systems in Java: abstract classes and interfaces. You will learn why we declare some types abstract, how abstract methods enforce subclass behavior, and how interfaces define reusable behavioral contracts. We'll examine practical examples, like a Shape hierarchy that defers area calculations to concrete shapes, and an Edible/Washable pair of interfaces that let unrelated classes share behavior. You'll also see how interfaces evolved in Java 8 to include default and static methods, and why that matters for A P I design. By the end of this chapter, you will understand when to provide a shared base implementation in an abstract class and when to expose a capability through an interface so classes can adopt it freely. We'll ground ideas with a hands-on payment processing exercise that demonstrates polymorphism: an Order uses a PaymentGateway contract to process payments without knowing gateway details. Notice how these patterns increase modularity, reduce duplication, and make code easier to extend. As you learn, ask yourself: would this behavior be better as a core identity of the type, or as an optional capability that many types may share?

In this set of objectives we make your outcomes explicit. First, you will learn to define and implement abstract classes: that means declaring a class as abstract, providing fields and concrete methods where appropriate, and declaring abstract methods that subclasses must implement. Practically, you'll apply this to examples like a Shape base class whose subclasses compute area. Second, you will create and use interfaces to describe behavior contracts. This includes writing interfaces, having classes implement them, and using those types polymorphically. Third, you will learn to differentiate when a design needs an abstract class versus an interface by examining their capabilities, inheritance rules, and common use cases. Finally, you'll begin to use Java 8+ interface features, implementing default and static methods when an interface benefits from a shared helper. Each skill reduces coupling and increases extensibility. As you progress, watch for the difference between owning state and declaring behavior: that distinction guides whether you choose an abstract class or an interface.

These objectives emphasize applying the chapter concepts in practical code. You will practice designing class hierarchies that use abstract classes for shared state and default behavior, and writing interfaces that represent capabilities such as Edible or Washable. You'll implement polymorphism by passing interface types into methods and letting different concrete classes behave differently at runtime. The hands-on activity in this chapter asks you to build a payment processing example that uses a PaymentGateway interface and multiple gateway classes; this trains you to depend on contracts rather than concrete implementations. You'll also practice avoiding common mistakes like attempting to instantiate an abstract class or forgetting to implement required methods. Finally, you'll reflect on design choices by classifying scenarios as better suited for an abstract class or an interface. These practice goals prepare you to design flexible, extensible Java systems in real projects.

An abstract class is a blueprint that cannot be instantiated directly and exists to be extended by concrete subclasses. It can contain fields, constructors, concrete methods with implementations, and abstract methods without bodies. Abstract methods declare a contract that subclasses must fulfill; if a subclass does not provide implementations for all inherited abstract methods, it must itself be declared abstract. This pattern is useful when there is a strong 'is-a' relationship and shared state or default behaviors belong on the base type. For example, a Shape abstract class can hold a color field, a constructor to set color, and a concrete displayColor method, while leaving calculateArea undefined so each concrete shape supplies its own formula. A common misconception is thinking abstract classes are only for uninstantiable objects — instead, emphasize they capture shared state and partial logic so subclasses avoid duplication. In practice, use abstract classes to centralize fields and default methods that truly belong to the base identity. Consider whether subclasses will share implementation or only behavior; that decision guides whether to make a base class abstract. What is an Abstract Class? means abstract classes bundle shared state and partial behavior while forcing subclasses to implement missing specifics.. In practical terms, a partially implemented type that defines a shared base and enforces contracts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through a concrete Shape example to see how abstract and concrete members coexist. The Shape class declares a protected color field and a constructor to initialize it. It declares an abstract method calculateArea, which has no body and signals that each concrete subclass must provide its own formula. At the same time Shape provides concrete methods like displayColor and getColor so subclasses inherit common behavior. A key point is that declaring even a single abstract method forces the class to be marked abstract. This design keeps area calculation specific to each shape while sharing color handling across all shapes. One misconception is thinking abstract methods are optional; they are not — concrete subclasses must implement them or be abstract themselves. In practice, this pattern reduces duplication because Circle and Rectangle inherit displayColor instead of reimplementing it. Consider how a new Triangle subclass would only add its own area logic while reusing Shape's color and display methods. This balance of enforced contracts and reusable logic is the main strength of abstract classes. Now let's examine concrete subclasses that extend an abstract class. Circle and Rectangle inherit Shape's color field and constructor behavior while providing their own state and concrete implementations of calculateArea. An interface is a contract that specifies behavior a class promises to provide. Historically, interfaces only declared abstract methods and constants. Classes implement interfaces and must provide concrete implementations for all abstract methods the interface declares. Let's summarize the core concepts to remember. An abstract class is a base that cannot be instantiated, can have fields and constructors, and mixes abstract methods with concrete implementations to share behavior. An abstract method declares a required behavior without an implementation and forces subclasses to implement it. An interface is a behavioral contract that classes implement; it now supports default and static methods which help evolve APIs safely. Remember that interface fields are public static final constants; interfaces do not hold instance state. Multiple inheritance of type is possible because a class may implement multiple interfaces, allowing it to be treated as several types. Keep these distinctions in mind when you design: choose abstract classes when shared state and identity matter; choose interfaces when you need composable capabilities across unrelated types. These choices help keep systems modular and easier to extend.

Keep three essentials close as you write Java code. First, abstract methods require implementation: any abstract method declared in a base type must be implemented by concrete subclasses or the subclass must be abstract. Second, use interfaces to express capabilities and enable a class to play multiple roles, such as Edible and Washable; this reduces coupling between producers and consumers of behavior. Third, Java 8's default and static methods let interfaces evolve safely, offering shared behavior or helpers without forcing all implementers to change. When you design, ask whether shared data is needed or if you only need to promise a behavior. That simple question guides whether a class should be abstract or whether an interface is the better tool. These three reminders will help you design clearer, more extensible object-oriented systems.
